In the model, these live trees are treated as pre-colonial reserve trees and represented with pre-colonial tree templates for the corresponding size class.



For senescing and snag, we use Killey et al. Table 7. This lets us define senescing as a portion of the live large-tree class, and snag as additional standing dead stems.9
Killey includes estmiates for a >60 cmtrunk size tree as 15 live stems/ha. These >60 cm stems are split into crown-condition classes:

11-12 of 15 live stems/ha are below 70% crown, which we treat as the broad senescing reference range.
4-6 of 15 live stems/ha are below 30% crown, which we treat as the severe senescing reference range.
3-6 dead stems/ha are present as standing dead trees, which we use as the snag reference range.

We define senescing as 65% of the live large cohort. This is a modelling value within the Killey-derived condition range below the broad 73-80% share of live >60 cm stems below 70% crown in Scenarios 1-2, but above the narrower 27-40% share below 30% crown. We do this because our large class is stricter than Killey et al.’s >60 cm class and so we use a conservative partition of the current live large cohort rather than adopting Killey’s 15 live stems/ha directly.

title: Appendix G - Pathway Simulation
text:
This appendix describes the simulation as implemented in _futureSim_refactored/.
This approach involves three key elements:

propositional community: generates proposals
evaluative community: negotiates differences and decides with mandate
pathways: show the visible consequences of these interactions over time






habitat feature is a composite volumetric description of a tree, log, pole, or artificial structure.
under canopy is the immediate space under or around a feature.
surrounding region is the larger connected region around a feature. [in the manuscript, drop this one]
expanded space is the connected space between features made available by the connectivity simulation.





Proposals can request:

modifications to existing habitat features that change their variant, such as Decay requesting a large feature continue to their senescing, snag and fallen lifecycle varient.
insertion of new habitat features such as sapling features under Recruit or artificial features under Deploy Structure.
modification to the expanded space that connects features, such as under Colonise.


Proposals are triggered by:

events (such as Decay)
latent changes (such as under Release Control)
respond to opportunities in environment (such as under Colonise responding to connectivity potential of the growth simulation)
or are enabled by previous proposals (such as Recruit and Deploy-Structure requesting insertion of new habitat features in areas unlocked by a previous Colonise proposal.

We model five proposals:

Individual tree features propose Decay when useful_life_expectancy reaches 0, requesting changes to the habitat feature, under canopy, and surrounding region that support progression through the lifecycle phases of senescing, snag, fallen, and decayed, or replacement.
Individual tree features propose Release Control at each pulse, requesting under canopy changes that support progression towards their moderated variant, and surrounding region changes that support progression towards their unmanaged variant.
Populations propose Colonise wherever the connectivity simulation makes expanded space available, requesting changes to ground, roof, and facade surfaces.
Populations propose Recruit at each pulse wherever Decay, Release Control, and Colonise have made under canopy, surrounding region, or expanded space available for new saplings.
Populations propose Deploy-Structure at compatible locations reached by Colonise, requesting changes that support artificial, hybrid, or fallen features.




Communities can fully or partially support proposals through Interventions. Interventions allow proposals to proceed (or modify them) through changes made to:

habitat features, such as brace partially supporting a Decay proposal.
the area immediatly under or around a habitat feature, such as buffer fully supporting a Decay proposal by converting this area into a habitat island
the area connecting features, such as modifications ground, roof, and facade surfaces in response to Colonise proposals.

The interventions we model are (broken down by their proposal family):
Decay - brace-feature provides partial support by retaining tree features through senescing and snag, but not collapse. - buffer-feature provides full support by modifying under canopy and surrounding region to support progression through fallen and decayed.
Release Control - reduce-canopy-pruning provides partial support by modifying under canopy to support progression towards a moderated variant. - eliminate-canopy-pruning provides full support by modifying the surrounding region to support progression towards an unmanaged variant.
Colonise - roughen-envelope provides partial support by converting facades in expanded space into biofacades, and rooftops into brown roofs. - enrich-ground provides full support by converting ground in expanded space into habitat ground. - enrich-envelope provides full support by converting load-bearing roofs in expanded space into green-roofs.
Recruit - rewild-smaller-patch provides partial support by inserting saplings in under canopy zones. - rewild-larger-patch provides full support by inserting saplings in under canopy linked, surrounding region, or expanded space.
Deploy-Structure - translocate-log provides full support by inserting fallen, or fallen and decayed, features. - adapt-utility-pole provides full support by inserting an artificial canopy feature. - upgrade-feature provides full support by converting an introduced tree to its hybrid variant.

fallen and decayed trees on colonised ground

title: Appendix G - Pathway Simulation
text:
habitat feature is a composite volumetric description of a tree, log, pole, or artificial structure.
under canopy is the immediate space under or around a feature.
surrounding region is the larger connected region around a feature. [in the manuscript, drop this one]
expanded space is the connected space between features made available by the connectivity simulation.





Proposals can request:

modifications to existing habitat features that change their variant, such as Decay requesting a large feature continue to their senescing, snag and fallen lifecycle varient.
insertion of new habitat features such as sapling features under Recruit or artificial features under Deploy Structure.
modification to the expanded space that connects features, such as under Colonise.


Proposals are triggered by:

events (such as Decay)
latent changes (such as under Release Control)
respond to opportunities in environment (such as under Colonise responding to connectivity potential of the growth simulation)
or are enabled by previous proposals (such as Recruit and Deploy-Structure requesting insertion of new habitat features in areas unlocked by a previous Colonise proposal.

We model five proposals:

Individual tree features propose Decay when useful_life_expectancy reaches 0, requesting changes to the habitat feature, under canopy, and surrounding region that support progression through the lifecycle phases of senescing, snag, fallen, and decayed, or replacement.
Individual tree features propose Release Control at each pulse, requesting under canopy changes that support progression towards their moderated variant, and surrounding region changes that support progression towards their unmanaged variant.
Populations propose Colonise wherever the connectivity simulation makes expanded space available, requesting changes to ground, roof, and facade surfaces.
Populations propose Recruit at each pulse wherever Decay, Release Control, and Colonise have made under canopy, surrounding region, or expanded space available for new saplings.
Populations propose Deploy-Structure at compatible locations reached by Colonise, requesting changes that support artificial, hybrid, or fallen features.




Communities can fully or partially support proposals through Interventions. Interventions allow proposals to proceed (or modify them) through changes made to:

habitat features, such as brace partially supporting a Decay proposal.
the area immediatly under or around a habitat feature, such as buffer fully supporting a Decay proposal by converting this area into a habitat island
the area connecting features, such as modifications ground, roof, and facade surfaces in response to Colonise proposals.

The interventions we model are (broken down by their proposal family):
Decay - brace-feature provides partial support by retaining tree features through senescing and snag, but not collapse. - buffer-feature provides full support by modifying under canopy and surrounding region to support progression through fallen and decayed.
Release Control - reduce-canopy-pruning provides partial support by modifying under canopy to support progression towards a moderated variant. - eliminate-canopy-pruning provides full support by modifying the surrounding region to support progression towards an unmanaged variant.
Colonise - roughen-envelope provides partial support by converting facades in expanded space into biofacades, and rooftops into brown roofs. - enrich-ground provides full support by converting ground in expanded space into habitat ground. - enrich-envelope provides full support by converting load-bearing roofs in expanded space into green-roofs.
Recruit - rewild-smaller-patch provides partial support by inserting saplings in under canopy zones. - rewild-larger-patch provides full support by inserting saplings in under canopy linked, surrounding region, or expanded space.
Deploy-Structure - translocate-log provides full support by inserting fallen, or fallen and decayed, features. - adapt-utility-pole provides full support by inserting an artificial canopy feature. - upgrade-feature provides full support by converting an introduced tree to its hybrid variant.

The engine assesses Deploy-Structure through four paths:

The model first calculates roof area, then how much additional log weight that roof can support per square metre.
green roof = 50 kg/m²; brown roof = 100 kg/m²
It multiplies that value by roof area to get the total log load the roof can carry.
It then assigns logs from the log library.
It tries large, then medium, then small.
It checks whether each log’s Biomass_kg fits within the remaining roof load.
If it fits, it accepts it and places it on a randomly chosen eligible roof voxel.
It continues until the remaining roof load is exhausted, or no more logs of that size can fit.

fallen and decayed trees on colonised ground

The model identifies colonised ground and calculates how much fallen and decayed deadwood can be inserted there in the current pulse.
It then adds new fallen and decayed features until that pulse budget is filled.

We use this clipped photomesh as an input into the voxel grid. This process generates voxels that define buildings in the habitat volume. We use the City of Melbourne development model (simplified building volumes) to segment individual buildings and provide surface orientation for voxels in the habitat volume. Assesses roof surfaces for structural capacity to support additional loads
Reads a log library cross-referenced to fallen tree habitat feature types, with mass per item and size class
Derives roof from the number of roof voxels and the voxel size
Computes a log load budget per roof based on structural capacity
Allocates logs to roof voxels while capacity remains

‘Birds’ persona includes woodland birds, including red-rumped parrot (Psephotus haematonotus) and Superb fairywren (Malurus cyaneus), represent social, intelligent canopy dwellers 1. The area of grassland (2.1.1) as well as the volume of dead branches (2.1.2) and epiphytes (2.1.3) in tree canopies relate to the lizard’s capability to forage (Figure 4, orange). Humans can enable opportunities for lizards to express this capability by converting ground surfaces to grasslands (2.1.1), releasing tree canopies from human control to allow dead branches to develop (2.1.2), and installing native mistletoe in tree canopies (2.1.3).
The area of unpaved ground relates to the lizard’s capability to explore (2.2.1) (Figure 4, pink). Humans can provide opportunities for exploration through removing hard surfaces. Sheltered sites including fallen nurse logs (2.3.1) and fallen trees (2.3.2) relate to the lizard’s capability to shelter (Figure 4, green). Humans can support this capability through retaining fallen branches (2.3.1) and trees (2.3.2) in situ.

title: Appendix A: Glossary
text:
The main text reframes several concepts to support our approach to nonhuman leadership. We provide a brief glossary of these terms here.



Community: In more-than-human terms (combining community ecology, political studies, etc), ‘community’ are practised relationships at a location, which create fuzzy, emergent groups consisting of humans as well as non-humans, refer 1.
Path: A depiction of a process that show changes to a community over time.
Possibility space: The search space that describes all possible paths.
Resistance: Multiple interacting constraints that make a path through the possibility space more or less likely. This includes functional, developmental, historical, genetic, political constraints and rigidity traps (ie. regulatory frameworks, time, and institutional capacity that lock managers into practices that appear safe but prevent adaptation). We implement resistance as a score from 0 to 100, where 0 indicates no resistance to change.
Destination: A potential (ie. probable, plausible, implausible, preferable) region of the possibility space.
Trend: The most likely path, ie. the path of least resistance.
Transformation: Fundamental shift away from the trend.
Pathway: An intentionally manipulated path created through a series of interconnected interventions aimed at reaching better destinations.





State: An observable instance along a path at a point in time.
Habitat volume: A way of representing a state as a three-dimensional grid of 25 × 25 × 25 cm cells, or “voxels”, each containing multiple attributes, an extension of prior work2. Habitat volumes are macroscale urban spatial units that include neighbourhoods or districts. Attributes express dynamic relationships defined by the participatory pipeline that include perching, sheltering and ageing in place. Our model assigns indicators to all habitat volumes deemed potentially “liveable” for the selected personas.
Habitat features: A way of differentiating the habitat volume. These aggregate habitat opportunities and represent vegetation, soil, water or artificial structures. Our current implementation focuses on trees.
Canopy footprint and patch resistance: The model aggregates resistance values to calculate “canopy footprint resistance” beneath habitat features and a “patch resistance” across building and ground surfaces. These metrics assess the effort required to create connections between features and support nonhuman proposals.





Design: The collective creation of conditions that support life in response to novelty.
Thriving: The measure we use to evaluate preferability along a path.
Intervention: Interventions are actions or strategies implemented to protect, restore, enhance, or manage biodiversity. They might include habitat restoration, species reintroduction, grazing management, or creation of artificial structures (e.g., nest boxes, deadwood habitats, green roofs) 3 as well as wildlife-friendly building standards, and biodiversity-inclusive approaches to urban planning, interventions into human behaviours or cultures such as through education or incentives.
Proposal: A way to sampling the possibility space. A possible way of living by individual or groups of community members. Proposals are the mechanisms where nonhuman beings identify ways of changing the habitat volume, either as individual organisms (as in the case of Elm personas proposing to complete full lifecycles) or as aggregated groups (Bird and Lizard personas proposing interventions such as depaving or deploying artificial trees
Effort: The degree of freedom interventions have to overcome resistance. We implement effort as thresholds (0-100) per intervention type, which determine a community’s capacity to consider and implement proposals. At each location, if resistance is less than or equal to the effort threshold, the community enables proposals through compatible interventions; if resistance exceeds the threshold, the community constrains proposals. Changes in effort thresholds over time reflect shifts in technology, understanding, costs, labour, or community perceptions. We vary effort at discrete points in time to define the conditions of a pathway. The model then calculates actualised interventions and the resulting pressure put on the path.
Leadership: An increase in the probability of thriving. We implement “leadership” as the likelihood that nonhuman proposals influence or redirect a pathway.





Place: A way to sample a community. Places are assemblages of abiotic and biotic interactions at a location.
Persona: A fictional representation of a community member based on quantitative data. We select “birds”, “lizards” and “trees” as urban taxa that persist at the case places and qualify as “ambassadors”. Our innovation is to treat nonhuman personas not as users but as co-designers, referred to as “designer personas”.
Capabilities: A way to measure of thriving. Capabilities are conditions that enable a persona to lead a good life.
Relational indicators: A way to track capabilities using measurable “indicators” that reflect liveable conditions for personas. We draw on ecological assessments of woodlands to define indicators as numerical expressions of relational capabilities. For example, the volume of dead branches may indicate birds’ capacity for perching and social interaction.
Experiences: Pathway states as encountered by personas. They concretise what it would be like for different community members (birds, lizards, trees, humans) to live in the modelled futures.

title: Appendix D: Habitat features
text:
The main article defines habitat features as aggregations of habitat opportunities derived from tree scans. This appendix provides further information on the numeric targets for calibration and the workflow to generate these features.


We derived habitat features from field scans of existing trees and modified them to represent four distinct origins.
Precolonial derives from scans of 16 Eucalyptus trees of species that dominated the open grassy woodlands that used to be widespread in south-eastern Australia1 and the northern parts of Melbourne2. These scans capture complex architecture that evolved over centuries without human interference.
Introduced derives from scans of 13 ageing Ulmus, including some of Melbourne’s oldest specimens. These represent introduced trees that now characterise urban forests.
Hybrid modifies “pre-colonial” or “introduced” by adding voxel attributes that refer to canopy upgrades such as artificial bark, prosthetic hollows, or planted mistletoe. This variant applies existing guidelines3 and emerging approaches explored in our previous work4.
Artificial modifies Eucalyptus voxel attributes to approximate properties of engineered canopy structures.

Next, we recognise “branch objects” in scanned trees. We call these recognised structures ‘branch objects’ to distinguish them from physical branches. We connect branch objects as topological networks and assign structural attributes including radius, length, position, their angles relative to the horizontal plane, and dead/alive states.  Figure 2. Initial segmentation of branch objects from scanned tree structure.
We then sample these connected branch objects as voels of 0.25m x 0.25m x 0.25m resolution. This provides sufficient detail to link spatial features in tree canopies with persona capabilities. This step transfers all attributes of branch objects into attributes of voxels, including the branch object to which each voxel belongs. This process accounts for external features on branches within trees including perch positions, dead branches, and leaf features but not internal features such as hollows.
We use the topological graph to group branch objects into communities that represent different canopy segments at multiple scales (Figure 3). Voxel-level: individual voxels
Branch-group level: voxels grouped by branch group
Canopy-group level: voxels grouped by three canopy groups

Count-based allocation assigns a specific number of features, where each feature corresponds to one branch group regardless of its voxel count.

title: Pathway simulation submodule A: Tree Growth
text:
We use allometric models to model empirically derived, size-dependent growth that accelerates early-life diameter accumulation and decelerates as trees mature.
The simulation engine supports multiple diameter-at-breast-height (DBH) growth models, selectable via the growth_model parameter. Each model computes new DBH values per simulation step using a virtual-age round-trip: the current DBH is mapped to an implied age, the age is advanced by the step duration, and the new age is mapped back to DBH.
A split mode applies different allometric curves to colonial and precolonial trees using the precolonial column in the tree dataframe, reflecting the different species composition of planted (predominantly elm) and remnant (predominantly eucalypt) urban trees.





The original v3/v4 growth model. Applies a fixed annual DBH increment equal to the mean of growth_factor_range (default 0.44 cm/yr) regardless of tree size.

Source: Not empirically derived. The value 0.44 cm/yr approximates observed growth rates for mature trees (DBH ~70–80 cm) but substantially underestimates growth for young trees.
Equation: \(\Delta\text{DBH} = \bar{g} \times \Delta t\), where \(\bar{g} = \text{mean}(\texttt{growth\_factor\_range})\).




Derived from Fischer et al. (2010) Supporting Information,1 which regressed tree age as a linear function of basal area using empirical data from Banks (1997).2 The regression was calibrated across multiple species standardised to yellow-box-equivalent diameters. Fischer report \(R^2 = 0.998\) (\(P < 0.0001\)).
This is the same equation used by Le Roux et al. (2014)3 to determine cohort residence times in their demographic model, from which our mortality rates are also derived. Using the Fischer growth curve therefore maintains internal consistency between the growth and mortality components of the simulation.

Equation: \(\text{Age} = 0.0197135 \times \pi \times (\text{DBH}/2)^2\)
Inverse: \(\text{DBH} = \sqrt{\text{Age} / k}\), where \(k = 0.0197135 \times \pi / 4 \approx 0.01548\)
Implied growth rate: \(d\text{DBH}/dt = 32.26 / \text{DBH}\) cm/yr

title: Pathway simulation submodule C: Recruit and mortality dynamics
text:
In addition to being differentiated by the size of the groundspace being made appropriate, support for the recruit proposal also changes the mortality of saplings, depending on whether it has full support (rewild ground intervention that opens larger swathes of ground to recruit) or partial (buffer tree only allowing recruitment under a selection of trees that have undergone buffer).
For mortality, we use two Le Roux data values that are described as derived from raw vegetation data or, where applicable, published estimates.1

annual_tree_death_urban = 0.06. Roughly 61% of trees survive over 8 years.2
annual_tree_death_nature-reserves = 0.03. Roughly 78% of trees survive over 8 years.3

We use annual_tree_death_urban by default and annual_tree_death_nature-reserves for tree mortality in larger rewilded areas to reflect these different conditions of proposals under recruit that are partially supported (smaller nodes, higher mortality) and fully supported (rewilded nodes, lower mortality). We also increase the density of plantings in the larger recruitment zones to reflect the increased support available in those areas.
In the current v4 implementation, we follow Le Roux’s cohort-thinning logic, keep their standard 0.06 urban and 0.03 nature-reserve annual mortality values as anchors, and apply DBH-cohort survival curves based on their assessments of tree survival across successive cohorts.

Our current recruit density is 50 trees/ha, but this is a pulse-scaled establishment value, not a final mature woodland density. In practice, that means:

10-year pulse = 16.7 trees/ha
20-year pulse = 33.3 trees/ha
30-year pulse = 50 trees/ha

This places the model on the assertive side, but still within the same broad range as several Australian woodland references.

Planting for Wildlife gives an open-woodland benchmark of about 30 mature trees/ha on pre-cleared hilltops and plains, with higher densities along watercourses.4
A Guide to Managing Box Gum Grassy Woodlands illustrates box-gum woodland at 35 trees/ha.5
The Future of Scattered Trees in Agricultural Landscapes uses 10-25 trees/ha as the initial yellow-box scattered-tree density. The same paper then models a stronger regeneration response of 2 recruits per initial tree every 30 years, so it supports low mature densities but also shows that recruit pulses can be substantially higher than the final standing structure.6
Reversing a Tree Regeneration Crisis in an Endangered Ecoregion is less useful as a direct density benchmark, but it is important context: the problem in these systems is not just low mature tree density but failed regeneration over time.7
The Future of Large Old Trees in Urban Landscapes reports 11-13 seedlings/ha in the 0-10 cm DBH cohort over an approximately 8-year step in urban greenspace.8 That is not the same thing as our planting quota, but it is the same order of magnitude. If our 50 trees/ha setting is treated as a 30-year establishment pulse, it scales to 13.3 trees/ha over 8 years, which is very close to Le Roux’s urban cohort figure.
